newsitem.title: USA: Foreign pests, disease threaten U.S. agriculture.
newsitem.headline: Foreign pests, disease threaten U.S. agriculture.

text.p: Federal inspectors who protect U.S. agriculture from foreign pests and diseases were struggling to keep up with rising international trade and taking dangerous shortcuts, a government report released Tuesday said.

In a critical look at the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), the General Accounting Office said the potential for dangerous outbreaks of foreign pests and diseases in the United States was likely to increase as global trade and travel expand.

"APHIS's inspection programme ... has not kept pace with the increasing pressure from its growing workload and mission," the GAO report said. "Heavy workloads have often led APHIS inspectors to shortcut cargo inspection procedures, thereby jeorpardizing the quality of the inspections conducted."

Every day, 2,700 APHIS officials inspect millions of tons of cargo and millions of people arriving at 172 ports of entry into the United States -- including airports, sea ports and border points with Mexico and Canada -- to prevent dangerous pests and diseases from coming into the country.
International cargo and goods entering the United States have grown rapidly since 1990, due in part to the North American Free Trade Agreement, the report said.

Investigators checked 11 U.S. ports of entry, including the Mexican border crossing, with the heaviest passenger vehicle volume in the nation. An APHIS department supervisor there said his staff was able to inspect fewer than 1 percent of the passenger cars that cross the border.
Some busy inspectors perform only "tailgate inspections" of goods stored near doors or openings, which often misses pests burrowed deeper into the cargo.

In Miami, the second busiest port in the nation, GAO investigators saw some APHIS inspectors allow importers of cut flowers to select their own samples for USDA inspection. "With this practice, brokers could select samples that are likely to pass inspection," the report said.

The report recommended that the USDA issue guidelines that outline minimum inspection standards for choosing inspection samples. Foreign pests and diseases entering the United States cost an estimated $41 billion annually in lost production and expenses for prevention, according to the USDA.
